Description of Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment and Controls The treatment system at the Facility consists of bar screening; biological treatment, including nitrification and denitrification; alkalinity adjustment; secondary sedimentation; cloth media filtration; and ultraviolet light (UV) disinfection. A 4-million-gallon emergency retention basin is available for storage of excess influent flow or partially treated wastewater. From January 2017 to December 2019, the maximum observed wet weather effluent flow was 5 MGD. Sludge processing consists of aerobic digestion and sludge storage basins. The sludge storage basins provide storage for stabilized solids during wet weather periods and serve as drying beds during the warm summer months. The facility produces approximately 158 dry metric tons of biosolids annually. Dried sludge is hauled to the West Central landfill, operated by the City of Redding, for disposal. B. chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: However, these processes are costly, require high energy consumption and generally produce secondary waste which cannot remove the pollutants completely and then puts more pressure on the environment (Ghafari et al., 2008; Kapoor and Viraraghavan, 1997) . In contrast, biological treatment is generally regarded as a better choice for nitrate removal from wastewater due to its advantages of complete contaminants removal, economical and energy-saving. Currently, the complete denitrification process is widely applied for nitrate-containing wastewater treatment (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) . However, the traditional complete denitrification process (Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 )) still presents some shortcomings, including high operational costs due to external organic carbon source requirements (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) , large amounts of sludge yields and inevitable greenhouse gas emission, etc. (Du et al., 2016b) . Partial denitrification (PD) refers to the process of controlling NO 3 − -N reduced to NO 2 − -N without further reducing to nitrogen gas (N 2 ).

chunks.text: The drying facility is located in a large Polish wastewater treatment plant and is composed of 4 lines. The scheme of one drying line is presented in Fig. 1 . Dewatered sludge is collected in a silo from where it is dosed to drum dryers. The temperature in the drum dryers is maintained at ca. 240-260 • C using hot oil. Sludge is uniformly distributed in the drum with paddles. The sludge retention time in the drier is 1-2 min, and the sludge layer in the drum is 1-2 cm thick. Water from the sludge is evaporated and flows as condensate with process air through a purification system composed of a Venturi orifice and two scrubbers, where it is then rinsed with the process water (secondary effluent from the wastewater treatment plant). chunks.text: Most biosolids in the US undergo anaerobic digestion; however, for smaller plants (less than 20,000 PE), aerobic digestion is more economical unless co-digesting with biowaste for energy recovery (Nowak et al., 2004) . Dewatering helps reduce the volume of sludge and, consequently, transportation costs. For the Beaver Dam WWTP, the biosolids from secondary digesters (2% solids) are land applied in neighboring farms during warm months (Beaver Dam, 2014) . When the land is frozen, the biosolids are dewatered by a belt filter press with polymer addition to achieve 12% solids concentration for onsite storage. The Delhi Charter Township WWTP in Michigan has a capacity of 15,000 m 3 /day (4.0 MGD) and implements energy and nutrient recovery (Viswanathan, 2010; Delhi, 2018) . Its biosolids handling capacity was increased from 45 to 114 m 3 /day (12,000 to 30,000 GPD) in 2007 and incorporated parallel treatment trains of two-phased anaerobic digesters that were capable of advanced, high-rate processing.

chunks.text: The secondary biological treatment consists of two carrousel-shaped biological reactors with suspended biomass, equipped with two horizontal aerators, which include nitrogen removal. Regarding the sludge line, a fraction of the solids settled in the secondary settler is purged to the sludge thickener. Previously to the band filter, the sludge passes through a homogenizer to be mixed with cationic polyelectrolyte and further dewatered in the band filter prior being stored in a silo. Calafell WWTP was built on 1994 to treat the wastewaters of the municipalities of Calafell and Bellveí and designed for 70,000 population equivalent with a maximum flow of 12,000 m 3 /day. After a primary treatment, wastewater is treated in two activated sludge reactors with extended aeration including nitrogen removal, followed by the secondary settler. From these units, the treated wastewater is directly discharged to the submarine sewage. Some differences are observed in the operation of the plant between winter and summer seasons due to fluctuations on the population and changes on the influent composition. A coagulation-flocculation treatment, only operated during summer, receives the wastewater after the screening step.

chunks.text: Continuing urbanization has placed a formidable burden on wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) (Du et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2019) . The development of innovative solutions that can intensify wastewater treatment processes becomes imperative. Anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) technology offers the potential to enhance wastewater treatment capacity owing to its remarkably reduced sludge production in a fully autotrophic nitrogen removal process (Jetten et al., 1997; Kuenen, 2008) . In addition, anammox processes have also demonstrated impressive high-rate capabilities, achieving nitrogen removal rates of up to 7.5 kg N/(m 3 d) in mainstream wastewater (Cheng et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2011; Yokota et al., 2018; Hou et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a) .
